<reason>A built the more effective practical case: concrete mechanisms (Terra's contagion, USDC/SVB de-peg, Tether's misrepresented reserves) showing that segregation/disclosure-style fixes did not actually prevent the failures CON pointed to. A's pressure questions forced CON either to concede that its "escalate when warranted" trigger has no detection mechanism besides examination, or to accept that reserve-investing issuers (i.e., virtually every real stablecoin) cross into fund-like territory by CON's own test. A honestly conceded a factual overstatement (Tether "collapse") when pressed, then pivoted cleanly, which is good epistemic discipline. The closing landed a genuinely decisive move: applying CON's own "invests backing assets" trigger to real-world issuers empties out CON's protected category, converting CON's principled distinction into a distinction without real-world difference. CON's rebuttals were competent and conceptually sound (ownership vs. access, activity vs. label, incumbency costs), and its final closing tried to salvage the point by reframing the debate as about future-proofing incentives rather than present issuers — a fair but more abstract move that doesn't fully answer why, for the motion as written, actual and foreseeable stablecoin issuers shouldn't get bank/MMF-style treatment. A's opening being clipped is a real execution cost, but the core content survived and A's later rounds compensated. Overall A had the sharper, more concrete, and more decisive path through the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal in [A2.2]-[A2.3], turning CON's own USDC/SVB example back on it (segregation didn't stop the run, and CON's proposed remedies wouldn't have helped because Circle wasn't insolvent, its custodian bank was), combined with the closing move in [A5.1]-[A5.2] showing CON's own "invests backing assets" trigger applies to every real issuer, forms the debate's decisive exchange.</best_rebuttal>
